title: Sorting: Bubble Sort
directAnswer: The number of swaps bubble sort performs equals the number of INVERSIONS in the array — pairs (i, j) with i < j but arr[i] > arr[j] — because each adjacent swap fixes exactly one inversion. Simulate bubble sort for O(n²), or count inversions with a modified merge sort for O(n log n).

remember.pattern: Bubble sort swap count = inversion count (merge-sort to count in O(n log n))
remember.formula:
swaps = number of pairs (i, j), i < j, arr[i] > arr[j]
O(n²): simulate bubble sort, ++swaps on every adjacent exchange
O(n log n): merge sort; while merging, when right element is taken before remaining left elements, add (mid - i + 1) to the count
rules: Each **adjacent** swap removes exactly **one** inversion — so total swaps = total inversions, independent of how bubble sort schedules them.
Bubble sort is O(n²) **comparisons** but the number of **swaps** can be anywhere from 0 (sorted) to n(n−1)/2 (reverse sorted).
Add an early-exit flag: if a full pass makes no swap, the array is already sorted — turns best case into O(n).
To count inversions fast, piggyback on **merge sort**: every time you pull an element from the right half before the left half is exhausted, it jumped over all remaining left elements.
Use a 64-bit accumulator — n(n−1)/2 for n = 10⁵ is ~5×10⁹, which overflows 32-bit int.
whenToUse: You need the count of adjacent swaps to sort, or 'how far from sorted is this array?'
A problem reduces to counting inversions (pairs out of order)
Teaching/derivation contexts where the bubble-sort ↔ inversions link is the point
Small n where O(n²) simulation is acceptable, or large n needing the merge-sort count
antiSignals: You only need the array sorted, not the swap count → use a real O(n log n) sort and move on
Swaps can be non-adjacent (selection-sort style) → swap count ≠ inversions
n is large and you simulate bubble sort → O(n²) will time out; count via merge sort
You forget the 64-bit accumulator → overflow on near-reverse-sorted big inputs
remember.takeaway: The headline result is bubble-sort swaps = inversions. Once you see that each adjacent swap fixes exactly one out-of-order pair, you can count swaps in O(n log n) with merge sort instead of simulating the quadratic process — a classic 'reframe the count' interview move.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you connect bubble sort's swap count to the number of inversions, and whether you know inversions can be counted in O(n log n) via merge sort rather than the obvious O(n²) simulation.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Counting comparisons instead of swaps, or assuming bubble sort always does ~n² swaps (it does ~n² comparisons but swap count depends on disorder), or overflowing int on large reverse-sorted inputs.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the invariant 'one adjacent swap removes exactly one inversion', conclude swaps = inversions, and offer the merge-sort O(n log n) count as the scalable alternative to simulation.

constraints: 1 ≤ a[i] ≤ 2·10⁹ (values can be large; comparisons only)
The array may already be sorted (0 swaps) or reverse sorted (n(n−1)/2 swaps)
The swap count can reach ~5×10⁹, beyond 32-bit int
understanding: Bubble sort repeatedly walks the array swapping any adjacent out-of-order pair, letting large elements 'bubble' to the end. We're asked only for how many such swaps happen — a quantity that equals the number of inversions in the original array.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we count swaps or comparisons?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Swaps. Comparisons are always ~n² here; swaps vary with how disordered the array is.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are swaps only between adjacent elements?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — bubble sort only ever exchanges neighbours. That's what makes swaps equal inversions.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can the answer get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to n(n−1)/2 for a reverse-sorted array. For n = 10⁵ that's ~5×10⁹, so use a 64-bit type.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the array guaranteed distinct?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not necessarily. Equal elements aren't inversions (we only swap on strictly greater), so define inversions with strict '>'.

approaches.name: Simulate Bubble Sort and Count (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Start here — it directly answers the question and proves the swaps-equal-inversions claim by construction.
hints: The problem literally gives you the algorithm. What's the most direct way to find the swap count?
Run the nested-loop bubble sort exactly as written and increment a counter on every swap.
Add an early-exit flag: if an entire inner pass performs no swap, the array is sorted and you can stop — this doesn't change the count but speeds up nearly-sorted inputs.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The outer loop runs up to n times and the inner up to n−1, so O(n²) comparisons. Swaps performed range from 0 to n(n−1)/2; we only use O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Run bubble sort precisely as specified: repeatedly sweep the array, and whenever `a[j] > a[j+1]`, swap them and increment a counter. After all passes the array is sorted and the counter holds the total swaps.

**Why this is the faithful baseline.** The prompt hands you the exact algorithm, so simulating it is unambiguously correct. It also *demonstrates* the key theorem rather than asserting it: every swap you count is an adjacent exchange that fixes one out-of-order neighbour pair.

**Why each swap removes exactly one inversion.** An inversion is a pair `(p, q)` with `p < q` and `a[p] > a[q]`. Swapping two *adjacent* elements `a[j]` and `a[j+1]` (because `a[j] > a[j+1]`) changes the order of only that one pair — every other pair keeps the same relative order, since their positions relative to each other are untouched. So one adjacent swap decreases the inversion count by exactly one. Bubble sort terminates when there are zero inversions (sorted), so the number of swaps it makes equals the number of inversions it started with — no more, no less.

**Why the early-exit flag matters.** Track whether the current pass made any swap. If a full pass is swap-free, the array is already sorted and the remaining passes would do nothing. This converts the best case (already sorted) from O(n²) to O(n) comparisons. It never changes the swap *count* — it just stops wasting comparisons.

**Why it doesn't scale.** The comparison work is quadratic regardless of the flag's help on adversarial inputs. At `n = 10⁵`, ~10¹⁰ comparisons is far too slow, which is why we reframe the count as inversions and use merge sort.
approaches.insight: Simulating bubble sort isn't just an answer — it's the proof. Watching each swap erase exactly one inverted neighbour pair is what licenses the leap to 'swaps = inversions', and from there to an O(n log n) count without simulating anything.

approaches.name: Count Inversions via Merge Sort (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The scalable answer. Phrase it as 'swaps equal inversions, and merge sort counts inversions in O(n log n)'.
hints: You've argued each adjacent swap kills one inversion, so the swap count equals the inversion count. Can you count inversions without sorting one swap at a time?
Merge sort splits the array, sorts each half, and merges. During the merge of two sorted halves, when do you learn that an element is out of order with several others at once?

When you take an element from the RIGHT half before the left half is exhausted, that right element is smaller than every remaining left element — so add (number of remaining left elements) to the inversion count.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Merge sort is O(n log n): log n levels of merging, each level touching all n elements once. The inversion counting adds only O(1) work per merge step. Temporary buffers cost O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Because bubble-sort swaps equal inversions, we can drop the simulation and just count inversions — and merge sort counts them almost for free while it sorts.

**The merge-sort counting trick.** Merge sort recursively sorts the left and right halves, then merges them into one sorted run. During the merge we have two pointers, one into the sorted left half and one into the sorted right half, and we repeatedly take the smaller front element. Here's the key: if the front of the **right** half is smaller than the front of the **left** half, then that right element is smaller than *every element still remaining in the left half* (the left half is sorted, so its front is its minimum). All of those remaining left elements originally sat *before* this right element but are *larger* than it — each is an inversion. So we add `(mid − i + 1)`, the count of remaining left elements, to the running total in one shot.

**Why this captures every inversion exactly once.** Any inverted pair `(p, q)` with `p < q` and `a[p] > a[q]` ends up with `a[p]` in some left half and `a[q]` in the corresponding right half at exactly one level of the recursion — the level where the split separates them. At that merge, `a[q]` is taken before `a[p]`, and `a[p]` is among the 'remaining left elements' counted. Pairs within the same half are counted deeper in the recursion. So each inversion is tallied once and only once.

**Why it's O(n log n).** The recursion has `log n` levels; each level merges disjoint runs covering all `n` elements, so each level is O(n). The inversion bookkeeping is a single addition per 'take from right' step, which doesn't change the asymptotics. This is the standard merge-sort cost, and it's the best achievable in the comparison model for counting inversions.

**Why the 64-bit accumulator is non-negotiable.** A reverse-sorted array of `n = 10⁵` has `n(n−1)/2 ≈ 5×10⁹` inversions, well past the 32-bit signed limit of ~2.1×10⁹. Accumulate in `long` (Java) — Python's integers are unbounded, so only Java is at risk.

**Why we still get the array sorted as a side effect.** The merge sort really does sort `a`; the inversion count is gathered along the way. If the caller also wants the sorted array (some variants ask for first/last element after sorting), it's already produced.
approaches.insight: The reframing — 'swaps = inversions' — is what unlocks the speedup. Once a quantity is recognised as an inversion count, merge sort (or a BIT/Fenwick tree) computes it in O(n log n). This same divide-and-conquer counting move solves Count of Smaller Numbers After Self and Reverse Pairs.

pitfalls: Using a[i] < a[j] instead of <= — counts equal elements as inversions, over-counting swaps.
Adding 1 per inversion instead of (mid − i + 1) — degrades to O(n²) and misses the batch insight.
Forgetting to copy the merged run back — parent merges then operate on unsorted halves and miscount.

commonMistakes: Counting comparisons rather than swaps — bubble sort always does ~n² comparisons.
Believing swap count is always ~n² — it equals inversions, which range from 0 to n(n−1)/2.
Overflowing a 32-bit counter on large reverse-sorted inputs.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Counting comparisons instead of swaps
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Incrementing on every comparison, not every actual exchange, reports ~n² regardless of disorder — the wrong quantity.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: 32-bit overflow on the swap count
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A reverse-sorted array of 10⁵ elements has ~5×10⁹ inversions, which wraps a 32-bit int negative.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Strict-less merge that miscounts equal elements
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Bubble sort swaps only on strictly greater, so equal elements are not inversions. Using a[i] < a[j] makes the merge take right elements on ties and over-count.

patternNote: Bubble-sort swaps = inversions, counted in O(n log n) by merge sort. Recognise the reframe whenever a problem counts adjacent exchanges or 'how unsorted' an array is. The merge-step counting trick generalises to Count of Smaller Numbers After Self and Reverse Pairs.
